Quoting myself below answering a similar question. This is the Electronic Frontier Foundation's review of the part that has been released so far. It's definitely worth a read.

tl;dr: It will deeply benefit giant corporations. They will get to have the power to sue the government for taking away profits, even if it's ridiculous. It's all about profit.

A favorite example of something that might happen is, let's say a private hospital is built by a huge medical corporation. A few years later, the state wants to build a new public hospital down the street because the city needs more hospital beds. The corporation that owns the private hospital can sue the state for "projected loss of profits." If the private company wins, the state doesn't get to build a hospital and might even have to pay the corporation for legal fees. Then the private hospital gets to profit from patients who have nowhere else to go. Even if the state wins, it would cost millions of taxpayer dollars for defense. Link to Julian Assange explaining the same thing.

Big Pharma would get to sue generic drug brands like Great Valu and Kirkland Signature for loss of profits, then jack up their own prices. Companies would be allowed to track everything you do on the internet so they can try to sell you more stuff (even more tracking than the relatively harmless cookies they already use). I've heard rumors (yes, just rumors until we get the full text) that something very similar to the grossly unpopular SOPA bill are included.

All these pieces come together to benefit giant corporations like Monsanto, Wal-Mart, etc. Therefore it also benefits politicians who accept bribes and other "gifts". There is a reason Canada was talking about loss of soveriegnty.

I believe the TPP is unconstitutional. I believe companies are not people. I do believe in globalization, but in a social sense, rather than a commercial one. This is a giant leap in the wrong direction.

The EFF article touches on:

  • Legally Binding Rules for Rightsholders, but only Soft Guidelines for Users

  • Expansion of Copyright Terms to 'life plus 70 years'

  • Ban on Circumventing Digital Rights Management (DRM) which are a bit harsh if you ask me

  • Criminal Enforcement and Civil Damages, similar to what I talk about in my quote, but about intellectual property

  • Top-Down Control of the Internet by forcing DNS's to publish information about who owns domains, as well as adopting "an equivalent to ICANN's flawed Uniform Domain-Name Dispute Resolution Policy (UDRP)"

  • ISP Liability, which will basically make all the trade countries adopt a system like the US's DMCA notice system
